# Methods — Semi-mechanistic (generation-interval) model of typhoid outbreak response immunization

*Draft Methods section for the revised manuscript. Equations are written in LaTeX and
render in Quarto/pandoc (→ Word, PDF, or HTML). Citation keys in square brackets are
keyed to the reference list at the end; two references flagged "[verify]" need their
author lists confirmed against the source.*

---

## 1. Choice of model structure

The impact of outbreak response immunization (ORI) can be evaluated with models spanning a
spectrum of mechanistic detail. At one extreme, a **static model** (our Equation 2 [Halloran
1991]) rescales the observed incidence curve by a fixed proportion after the vaccine takes
effect; it makes no representation of transmission. At the other extreme, a **fully mechanistic
compartmental model** (e.g., a susceptible–exposed–infectious–carrier–recovered structure with
an environmental reservoir [Pitzer 2014; Watson 2015]) represents the transmission process
explicitly. Between these lies the **renewal-equation (generation-interval) framework**
[Wallinga 2004; Cori 2013; Champredon 2018], which represents transmission through a single
time-varying reproduction number and the generation-interval distribution, without committing
to a specific compartmental mechanism.

We adopt the renewal framework as the dynamic complement to our static primary analysis, for
four reasons specific to the data and the pathogen.

**(i) A single outbreak does not identify a mechanistic model.** Each outbreak trajectory
carries roughly four pieces of information — the initial growth rate, the timing and height of
the peak, and the rate of decline. A mechanistic typhoid model of the type required to represent
this disease faithfully (direct and environmental transmission, a chronic-carrier reservoir, and
age structure) contains on the order of ten to twenty parameters, together with unobserved
initial conditions. Fitting such a model to one outbreak requires fixing almost all parameters
from external literature and estimating only one or two; the resulting "fit" is then largely a
restatement of the priors rather than an inference from the data. The renewal equation extracts
the same growth-and-decline information non-parametrically, through the reconstructed
reproduction number $R_t$, and requires only the generation-interval distribution as a
transmission assumption.

**(ii) The classic typhoid non-identifiability is not resolved by adding mechanism.** From
incidence data alone, the reporting fraction, the initial susceptible fraction, and the
transmission rate are jointly non-identifiable: they trade off to produce identical epidemic
curves [Watson 2015]. A mechanistic model does not resolve this confounding; it relocates it into
the prior distributions. The renewal approach sidesteps it: $R_t$ absorbs the product of the
transmission rate and the susceptible fraction, and — because the proportional impact measures
are invariant to a time-constant reporting fraction (Section 5) — the percent-case-reduction
estimand does not require the reporting fraction to be known.

**(iii) An outbreak is the wrong regime for an endemic-equilibrium model.** Published mechanistic
typhoid models are calibrated to endemic, multi-year, age-stratified incidence with steady-state
carrier and environmental reservoirs [Pitzer 2014; Phillips 2020]. An outbreak — frequently a
transient, point-source waterborne event with an attack rate of approximately 1% (Results) — is
precisely the regime in which the endemic-equilibrium structure is least constrained by the data
and most prone to misspecification. The low attack rate is informative: it implies that
susceptible depletion over the outbreak is negligible ($S(t)/N \approx \text{const}$), so the
observed decline in transmission reflects the public-health response (chlorination, WASH, source
remediation) rather than depletion of susceptibles. This is the regime in which the principal
added value of a compartmental model — its nonlinear depletion dynamics — is smallest, and in
which the renewal equation is most accurate.

**(iv) The renewal equation is the mechanistic model, reduced.** This is the central point.
Champredon, Dushoff and Earn [Champredon 2018] proved that the renewal equation produces
**identical dynamics** to an Erlang-distributed SEIR (and SIR) compartmental model when the
generation-interval distribution used in the renewal equation is the intrinsic generation
interval implied by the model — namely, the convolution of the latent-period and
infectious-period distributions [Svensson 2007; Champredon 2015]. The renewal framework is
therefore not an alternative to mechanistic modeling but its formal reduction in the regime our
data occupy: the compartmental structure that one outbreak cannot identify is integrated out,
while the transmission dynamics that the data *can* inform are retained in $R_t$. Choosing the
renewal model is thus a statement about the information content of the data, not a concession of
rigor — and for the present comparative, multi-outbreak analysis it places the model at the
appropriate level of complexity.

Applying nineteen separate mechanistic models would, in addition, require nineteen sets of
largely unidentifiable parameter choices, undermining the comparability that motivates the study.
The renewal procedure is identical across outbreaks, with all between-outbreak heterogeneity
captured transparently by the reconstructed $R_t$ trajectories.

A consequence of the resolution analysis (Supplementary Methods) is that the renewal model is
applied only to outbreaks whose reporting interval $\Delta$ is short relative to the generation
interval $\mu_g$. The instantaneous reproduction number is identifiable from incidence only when
the generation interval spans several observation steps; when $\Delta \gtrsim \mu_g$, successive
transmission generations collapse into a single reporting interval and $R_t$ degenerates to a
ratio of consecutive counts that conflates generations. With a typhoid generation interval of
about two weeks (Section 4), this criterion ($\mu_g/\Delta \gtrsim 2$) is met by the outbreaks
reporting daily and weekly incidence ($n=13$) and fails for those reporting monthly incidence;
the renewal analysis is therefore restricted to the former, while the static analysis, which is
robust to reporting resolution, is applied to all outbreaks.

---

## 2. The two-level additive renewal model

We use additive models at two distinct levels. At the **observation level**, reported suspected
febrile cases $S_t$ are the sum of true symptomatic typhoid cases $T_t$ and other febrile cases
$F_t$:

$$
S_t = T_t + F_t,\qquad
\frac{\sum_t T_t}{\sum_t S_t}=\pi ,
$$

where $\pi$ is the positive predictive value (PPV) of the suspected-case definition. The primary
allocation estimates a non-negative approximately flat other-febrile background, truncates it
where necessary, and renormalizes $T_t$ so its cumulative fraction is exactly $\pi$. The resulting
$F_t=S_t-T_t$ is held fixed under vaccination. Thus vaccination changes true typhoid, not unrelated
febrile illness; the percentage reduction in suspected cases is consequently diluted when PPV is
low.

At the **transmission level**, true typhoid incidence is itself the additive sum of exogenous
background or common-source incidence $X_t$ and propagated incidence $P_t$:

$$
T_t = X_t + P_t,\qquad
P_t = R_t^{P}\Lambda_t,\qquad
\Lambda_t=\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}w_sT_{t-s}.
$$

Both components are true typhoid and therefore both contribute to later infectiousness
$\Lambda_t$. The sequence $\{w_s\}_{s\ge1}$ is the discretized generation-interval probability
mass function ($\sum_{s\ge1}w_s=1$). The structural source fraction $\theta$ is used to allocate
renewal-identifiable baseline incidence within this additive recursion,
$X_t=\theta T_t$ and $P_t=(1-\theta)T_t$, with
$R_t^P=P_t/\Lambda_t$. When $\Lambda_t=0$ but $T_t>0$, incidence is necessarily treated as an
exogenous seed ($X_t=T_t$, $P_t=0$). This seed rule preserves baseline mass and avoids discarding
the first generation.

**Generation-interval discretization.** The continuous generation-interval density is taken to be
gamma-distributed with mean $\mu_g$ and standard deviation $\sigma_g$ (Section 4), with
cumulative distribution $G$. It is discretized to the reporting interval $\Delta$ as

$$
w_s \;=\; \frac{G(s\Delta) - G\big((s-1)\Delta\big)}{1 - G(0)}, \qquad s = 1, 2, \ldots,
$$

with $w_0 = 0$ (no transmission in zero elapsed time). For the production analysis we use the
refined discretization of Cori et al. [Cori 2013], which accounts for infection times being
distributed within, rather than at the edge of, each interval; for a two-week mean generation
interval the choice of discretization has negligible effect on the results.

This construction is self-consistent: $X_t+R_t^P\Lambda_t=T_t$ at baseline. EpiEstim estimates of
$R_t$ are retained as a diagnostic cross-check, but the intervention recursion uses the exact
baseline reconstruction above. Uncertainty in PPV, vaccine efficacy, coverage, campaign timing,
generation interval, and $\theta$ is propagated with paired Sobol draws.

---

## 3. How the vaccine reduces the two typhoid components

The ORI campaign is delivered at time $\tau$, and protection develops after the rollout and
immunity-onset delay. Let $c(t)\in[0,1]$ be the protected fraction of the target population by time
$t$, $\kappa$ the final coverage, and $\psi_T$ vaccine efficacy against symptomatic typhoid. The
remaining susceptibility multiplier is

$$
q_t=1-c(t)\kappa\psi_T.
$$

Vaccination acts on both additive typhoid components because both represent vaccine-preventable
typhoid:

$$
X_t^v=q_tX_t,\qquad
P_t^v=q_tR_t^P\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}w_sT_{t-s}^v,\qquad
T_t^v=X_t^v+P_t^v.
$$

The factor $q_t$ directly protects vaccinated people against background/common-source exposures
and against propagated exposures. In addition, each propagated case averted reduces infectiousness
in later intervals, generating indirect protection endogenously. No fixed indirect-effect
parameter is imposed. The counterfactual suspected-case series is
$S_t^v=T_t^v+F_t$; other febrile illness remains unchanged.

**Impact measures.** Cumulative cases averted and the percent case reduction are

$$
A_T=\sum_t(T_t-T_t^v),\qquad
\rho_T=\frac{A_T}{\sum_tT_t}\times100\%,\qquad
\rho_S=\frac{A_T}{\sum_tS_t}\times100\%.
$$

The same true-typhoid cases averted feed the disability-adjusted-life-year and cost calculations.

---

## 4. Generation-interval parameterization

The generation-interval distribution is the only transmission assumption the renewal model
requires, and it is the principal source of structural uncertainty; we therefore parameterize it
explicitly from the natural history of typhoid and subject it to sensitivity analysis.

Under the compartmental interpretation, the intrinsic generation interval is the convolution of
the latent period (infection to onset of infectiousness) and the infectious-period profile
(weighted by the intensity of onward transmission) [Svensson 2007; Champredon 2015; Champredon
2018]. For typhoid these components are characterized as follows. The **latent period is short**:
*S.* Typhi can be shed in stool within approximately 24 hours of infection [Marudaiappan 2021,
verify]. The **incubation period** (infection to symptom onset), which governs when cases are
detected rather than when they transmit, has a usual range of 8–14 days, with a plausible range of
3–60 days; a systematic review and meta-analysis estimated subgroup mean incubation periods of
9.7–21.2 days [BMC Infect Dis 2018, doi:10.1186/s12879-018-3391-3, verify]. **Onward transmission**
occurs across the acute and early convalescent phases, during which shedding is highest; in a
household study of culture-confirmed paediatric cases, shedding persisted for a median of
approximately 11 days (range 3–61) and secondary shedding was detected in about 20% of case
households [Marudaiappan 2021, verify]. A small fraction of cases (roughly 1–4%) become chronic
carriers and contribute a long right tail to the distribution, although carriage contributes
principally to endemic maintenance rather than to the dynamics of a single outbreak.

Combining a short latent period with an infectious profile concentrated in the symptomatic acute
phase yields a base-case mean generation interval of approximately **two weeks**. This is
consistent with, and bounded above by, the **four-week generation interval** adopted in
endemic typhoid time-series SIR models [Phillips 2020]. Because direct empirical estimates of the
typhoid generation interval are scarce, we adopt a gamma distribution with a base-case mean of
$\mu_g = 14$ days and explore $\mu_g \in [7, 28]$ days (1–4 weeks) in sensitivity analysis, with
the standard deviation set to give a coefficient of variation of approximately 0.6 to reflect the
substantial individual variation in incubation and shedding.

| Natural-history component | Value (range) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Latent period (infection → shedding) | ~1 day | Marudaiappan 2021 [verify] |
| Incubation period (infection → symptoms) | 8–14 d usual; subgroup means 9.7–21.2 d | BMC Infect Dis 2018 [verify]; CDC |
| Acute/convalescent shedding (onward transmission) | median ~11 d (3–61) | Marudaiappan 2021 [verify] |
| Chronic carriage (right tail) | ~1–4% of cases | shedding/carriage reviews |
| **Generation interval, base case** | **mean 14 d (gamma, CV ≈ 0.6)** | derived (this study) |
| Generation interval, sensitivity range | mean 7–28 d (1–4 wk) | bounded above by Phillips 2020 |

## 5. Comparison with the historical weighted and fully mechanistic models

The models differ in *what the vaccine acts on*, where source contributions enter, and how
indirect protection arises. These differences are summarized in Table M1.

**Static model (Equation 2).** The static model multiplies true typhoid incidence after
$t^\ast$ by a fixed factor $1-P$, where $P$ combines direct and externally specified indirect
effects under the Halloran formulation [Halloran 1991]:

$$
T_t^{\mathrm{static}} = T_t\big[\,1 - \mathbb{1}(t\ge t^\ast)\,P\,\big],
\qquad
P = 1 - (1-\eta)(1-\kappa\psi_T),
\qquad
A^{\mathrm{static}} = P\!\!\sum_{t\ge t^\ast}\! T_t.
$$

The indirect effectiveness $\eta$ enters as an **exogenous constant**, independent of coverage and
of epidemic phase; the shape of the post-intervention curve is held fixed and only its height is
scaled; and there is **no transmission feedback** — averting a case in one interval does not
reduce incidence in the next. The static model thus measures a one-shot reduction of the
true-typhoid curve.

**Additive renewal-with-source model (primary).** The primary model applies the direct vaccine
effect to both $X_t$ and $P_t$ and allows only $P_t$ to compound through transmission feedback.
This is not a numerical blend of two completed counterfactuals: the components interact inside
one recursion because all earlier true typhoid cases contribute to $\Lambda_t$.

**Historical $\theta$-weighted model (comparison only).** Earlier analyses instead computed a
static counterfactual and a pure-renewal counterfactual separately and averaged their impact:

$$
A_{\mathrm{weighted}}
=\theta A_{\mathrm{static}}+(1-\theta)A_{\mathrm{renewal}}.
$$

That expression is retained solely to quantify the effect of changing model structure. It is not
the primary analysis because it combines outcomes after simulation and therefore does not preserve
the additive incidence identity $T_t=X_t+P_t$ or the shared infectiousness history. Paired
simulations use the same PPV, timing, coverage, efficacy, generation interval, and $\theta$ draws,
so their difference isolates the structural change.

In the paired base-case simulation across 13 renewal-eligible outbreaks, the additive model
reduced true typhoid by 25.6%, compared with 25.9% under the historical weighted calculation.
The additive-minus-weighted difference was -0.5 percentage points (95% simulation interval -2.4
to 0.7), or -37 cases (-212 to 52). Although the pooled estimates were close, outbreak-specific
differences were larger and could occur in either direction because the shared recursion changes
the timing of feedback.

**Fully mechanistic model.** A representative compartmental structure for typhoid tracks
susceptible ($S$), exposed ($E$), infectious ($I$), chronic-carrier ($C$) and recovered ($R$)
populations together with an environmental reservoir ($W$):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot S &= \mu(N-S) - \lambda(t)\,S, &
\dot E &= \lambda(t)\,S - (\sigma+\mu)E, &
\dot I &= \sigma E - (\gamma+\mu) I, \\
\dot C &= \theta\gamma I - \mu C, &
\dot R &= (1-\theta)\gamma I - \mu R, &
\dot W &= \xi\,(I + \rho_C C) - \delta_W W,
\end{aligned}
$$

with force of infection combining direct and environmental routes,
$\lambda(t) = \beta_I I/N + \beta_W\, W/(K_W + W)$. In this model the vaccine moves a fraction
$\kappa\psi_T$ of $S$ into the immune class (and could, in principle, additionally reduce shedding $\xi$
or carrier formation $\theta$), and indirect protection emerges mechanistically and
route-specifically. The cost of this fidelity is the parameter set
$\{\beta_I, \beta_W, \sigma, \gamma, \theta, \rho_C, \xi, \delta_W, K_W\}$, the initial conditions
$\{S_0, E_0, I_0, C_0, W_0\}$, and the reporting fraction — far exceeding what a single outbreak
can identify (Section 1). By the equivalence of [Champredon 2018], in the low-depletion limit with
the intrinsic generation interval set to the convolution of the $E$ and $I$ sojourn-time
distributions, this system reduces exactly to the renewal model of Section 2.

**Table M1. Comparison of the modelling approaches.**

| Property | Static | Historical weighted comparator | Additive renewal-with-source (primary) | Full mechanistic SEIR–carrier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quantity modelled | true-typhoid cases, rescaled | weighted completed impacts | $T_t=X_t+P_t$ inside one recursion | compartmental flows $S,E,I,C,R,W$ |
| Vaccine acts on | cases after $t^\ast$ | static and pure-renewal arms separately | both source and propagated typhoid; feedback through propagated cases | susceptibles; optionally shedding/carriage |
| Indirect protection | exogenous fixed $\eta$ | inherited from separate arms | endogenous, coverage- and phase-dependent | endogenous, route-specific |
| Transmission feedback | none | only in pure-renewal arm | yes, within additive recursion | yes, nonlinear |
| Source contribution | not separated | post hoc weight $\theta$ | additive incidence component $X_t$ | explicit source processes |
| Other febrile illness | held fixed | held fixed in paired comparison | held fixed | outside transmission system |
| Identifiable from one outbreak? | no fitting | $\theta$ externally classified | $R_t^P$ reconstructed conditional on external $\theta$ | generally no |

---

## 6. Limitations of the renewal approach

The first additive level assumes that non-typhoid febrile illness is unaffected by ORI and uses an
approximately flat allocation in time; PPV identifies the cumulative amount of true typhoid but
not its week-specific allocation. At the second level, $\theta$ is externally informed by outbreak
source classification because curve shape alone did not identify its level reliably. The
generation-interval kernel is a reduced-form summary of propagated transmission routes and does
not represent route-specific vaccine effects. Holding $R_t^P$ fixed under the counterfactual does
not re-inflate transmission to credit susceptibles preserved by vaccination; at the low attack
rates observed this depletion feedback is second-order. The model also does not mechanistically
represent chronic-carrier dynamics or a persistent environmental reservoir. Finally, renewal
analysis is restricted to outbreaks reported at a resolution fine relative to the generation
interval.
